findings.title: No App Store screenshots exist, and the only candidates (the design mirrors) cannot be used
findings.claim: ASC will not accept a first submission without at least one iPhone screenshot at 6.9" or 6.5" size. Nothing real has ever been captured. The 20 PNGs in docs/claude-design-handoff/screenshots/ are all 920x1840, which is not an accepted size (the aspect is 1:2, while Apple's sizes are about 1:2.17). They are also web mock-ups: they show a drawn device frame, a fake 9:41 status bar, grey placeholder product images and made-up figures ('329 BHD' vs '299 BHD', '2,000+ shoppers in Capital leaned the same way'). Uploading them would break 2.3.3 (screenshots must show the app in use) and 2.3 (accurate metadata). The Results screen, the most important one to show, cannot be captured today either, because a live compare returns HTTP 400 while OpenAI is out of quota. The screenshot section of the existing checklist is also stale: it uses the old 6.7"/12.9" names and lists the onboarding loading screen, which is a splash-type screen that 2.3.3 excludes.

(1) Apple's screenshot specifications page (fetched 2026-09-29) says the 6.5" set is "Required if app runs on iPhone and screenshots for 6.9" display aren't provided". The accepted sizes are 1260x2736, 1290x2796 and 1320x2868 for 6.9", and 1284x2778 and 1242x2688 for 6.5". It also says "Images cannot include alpha channels or transparencies."

(2) I measured the PNG headers myself. Every file in docs/claude-design-handoff/screenshots/ is 920x1840, which is not an accepted size. loading.png is colour type 6 (RGBA). There are 22 files, not 20. They were drawn by docs/claude-design-handoff/render-screenshots.js, so they are design renders, not captures from the running app.

(3) App Review Guideline 2.3.3, quoted verbatim: "Screenshots should show the app in use, and not merely the title art, login page, or splash screen." That rules out using the mock-ups as captures of the real app. It also rules out the "theatrical loading" onboarding screen, which is listed in both docs/plans/bundle-d-asc-submission-checklist.md:218-219 and docs/runbooks/bundle-d-screenshot-capture.md (capture #2).

The finding leaves this out, and its fix only covers a physical iPhone, which cannot produce the iPad images. Ahmed needs either an iPad capture path (a real iPad, or a Mac simulator via a --simulator build) or a product call to set supportsTablet to false before the production build.

(5) The Results screen cannot be captured while OpenAI is out of quota (the orchestrator measured the HTTP 400).

(6) There is also an existing runbook, docs/runbooks/bundle-d-screenshot-capture.md, that assumes Xcode and the iOS Simulator. That does not work on this Windows machine, so it is stale in the same way as the checklist.

Conclusion: severity blocker is correct, because ASC will not let a first version be submitted without the required screenshot sets. Owner ahmed is correct (credits, a phone or iPad, and possibly the tablet call). Claude can do the resize, alpha stripping and captions.

findings.title: A fake subscription paywall is reachable in the app: priced plans, a '3-Day Free Trial' CTA, invented social proof, and every button shows 'Coming soon'
findings.claim: The Paywall route is always registered. The Profile row 'Upgrade to Premium' opens it, and so do seven HomeScreen/ResultsScreen paths once the free quota runs out (3 per day, 3 lifetime-free). A reviewer will reach it. The screen shows BHD prices and a free trial that does not exist, and every CTA (Start trial, Terms, Privacy, Restore) only opens a 'Coming soon' alert. It also shows 'Trusted by 5,000+ GCC shoppers' and a 4.8-star rating for an app that has never shipped. This breaks 2.1(a) (incomplete feature and placeholder), 2.3.1(a) (promoting services it does not offer), and 3.1.1/3.1.2 (a subscription offered without in-app purchase). The ToS also promises 'Premium subscribers'.

votes.reasoning:
I read the code on main (C:/Users/SynAckITPC/Documents/AI/smartcompare) and fetched the App Review Guidelines. The finding holds.

What the code shows:
- **The route is always registered.** App.tsx:454-455 registers Paywall with no flag gating it.
- **Profile entry:** ProfileScreen.tsx:465-468 is an unconditional "Upgrade to Premium" row.
- **Home and Results entries:** HomeScreen.tsx has seven navigate('Paywall') calls (354, 467, 508, 588, 614, 677, 814). ResultsScreen.tsx:317 adds one more.
- **The header path is wider than the finding says.** HomeScreen.tsx:812-814 (handleHeaderCounterPress) opens the Paywall on any tap of the header counter, whether or not quota remains.

What the screen shows:
- Yearly "0.9 BHD/mo" with "3 DAYS FREE · BEST VALUE", and Monthly "2.9 BHD" (PaywallScreen.tsx:287-307).
- A trial timeline, "Today… In 3 days · Billing starts" (PaywallScreen.tsx:331-367).
- A CTA reading "Start My 3-Day Free Trial" and "No payment due now · Cancel anytime" (PaywallScreen.tsx:369-393).
- Social proof: a hardcoded "5,000+" and "4.8" (PaywallScreen.tsx:139-145).
- Every CTA, plus the Terms, Privacy and Restore links, only calls Alert.alert('Coming soon'). The CTA handler is at PaywallScreen.tsx:233-243; the links use onComingSoon at 396-406.
- Free quota: TIER_LIMITS free lifetime_free 3 / daily 3 / monthly 10 (app/services/usage_service.py:138-143).
- The ToS promises "Premium subscribers earn 10 per conversion" (app/legal/terms_of_service.md:85).

Apple sources (https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/):
- **2.1(a):** "placeholder text, empty websites, and other temporary content should be scrubbed before submission". A visible upgrade flow whose every button says "Coming soon" is temporary content, and reviewers routinely reject this under 2.1.
- **2.3.1(a):** "marketing your app in a misleading way, such as by promoting content or services that it does not actually offer … or promoting a false price … is grounds for removal". That fits a priced plan and trial that do not exist. The invented 5,000+ users and 4.8 rating are also dishonest marketing in the sense of 2.3.1(b): "if you're dishonest, we don't want to do business with you."

Where the finding overreaches:
- **3.1.1 / 3.1.2 is the weakest cited basis.** No purchase actually happens, so no non-IAP unlock mechanism exists, and 3.1.2's disclosure rules apply to real subscriptions. What would actually get this rejected is 2.1(a) plus 2.3.1(a).
- **"Seven HomeScreen/ResultsScreen paths" miscounts slightly.** It is seven in HomeScreen plus one in ResultsScreen.

Severity and owner:
- **Blocker is justified.** A reviewer who opens Profile, or taps the Home header counter, lands on this screen without running out of quota.
- **Owner "claude" is right for the code work:** the screen, the Profile row, the header counter and the i18n EN/AR keys are repo JS changes. They must ship in the production binary, not only through the preview OTA.
- **The ToS line needs Ahmed.** It lives in legal text that is still an unfinalized draft, so its wording is his legal call, while the code removal is Claude's.

1. The quote "(all 1024x1024, mode P, no transparency)" is wrong for two of the files. splash-icon.png and adaptive-icon.png both carry a tRNS transparency chunk. Only icon.png has none. Making the files byte-distinct and flipping ICON_ART_SUPPLIED satisfies the repo's own test, not App Review. The guideline citation is wrong, and I would not call this a blocker.
(1) Guideline 2.3.8 covers age-appropriate icons and icon/name consistency ("adhere to a 4+ age rating... app name and icons... are similar to avoid creating confusion"). Guideline 4.0 is a general design preamble. Neither one targets placeholder art. The rule that does is 2.1(a), App Completeness: "Submissions to App Review... should be final versions with all necessary metadata... placeholder text, empty websites, and other temporary content should be scrubbed before submission" (developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/, fetched 2026-09-29).
(2) The wording is "should". A placeholder icon is not rejected automatically. A human reviewer may reject under 2.1 or 4.0, but outcomes vary, so this is a likely rejection rather than a certain one. CLAUDE.md:13 says "Apple's automated review will reject", which overstates it. That puts it at high, not blocker. It is still a must-fix before submission, and it has to land before the production eas build.

The fix is also wrong in a way that matters. CLAUDE.md:13 and the finding both frame the problem as byte-identity and suggest re-rendering "the same visual" (the concentric-circles design Ahmed approved) with an emerald accent. But the approved design is the Expo template image. A reviewer judges the pixels, not the SHA-256, so a unique re-render of concentric circles would still look like the stock placeholder. The real fix is brand art: a Qaren/قارن wordmark or glyph on an opaque 1024x1024 PNG with no alpha. Only Ahmed can make that call, so the owner should be ahmed for the decision. Claude can execute once the art is chosen, either by rendering it with PIL or by exporting from Claude Design, then writing three distinct files, flipping ICON_ART_SUPPLIED and running jest. So "either" is only partly right.

The splash and adaptive icons being byte-identical is simply how the Expo template ships. It is not a separate problem and does not by itself show there is no custom art.

findings.title: OpenAI credits are exhausted, so every compare path the reviewer uses fails, including the mobile app's own explicit-pair and SSE paths
findings.claim: With OpenAI returning 429 insufficient_quota, no compare path produces a result. The orchestrator already measured the q= path (HTTP 400). I also measured the paths the app itself uses (it sends product_a/product_b). The explicit-pair GET ran the whole paid scrape cascade and returned HTTP 400 INSUFFICIENT_DATA after 31.2 s, with copy telling the user to choose different products. The SSE stream, which is the app's primary route, returned STREAM_TIMEOUT after 33.9 s with 'give it another tap in a moment', and retrying cannot help. The camera path (identify_products) catches only JSONDecodeError, so the 429 surfaces as HTTP 500 'Image analysis failed'. The URL compare returns LLM_UNAVAILABLE. A reviewer who exercises the core feature sees it fail every time (App Review Guideline 2.1, App Completeness).

evidence.quote: HTTP 400 in 31.2 s {"success":false,"error":"Comparison data was incomplete — choose different products.","code":"INSUFFICIENT_DATA"}
event: complete data: {"success": false, "error": "Still gathering prices — give it another tap in a moment.", "code": "STREAM_TIMEOUT", "partial": true, "elapsed_seconds": 33.17022
params.set('product_a', input.product_a.trim()); ... `${API_BASE_URL}/api/v1/text/compare/stream?${params.toString()}`
vision_result = await identify_products(image_data_list) except Exception as e: ... raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Image analysis failed. Please try again.")
openai.RateLimitError: 429 {'type': 'insufficient_quota', 'code': 'credit_balance_exhausted'} ... three attempts per call (SDK default retries)

findings.fix: Ahmed: (1) in the OpenAI dashboard, read Settings → Limits and record the tier and the gpt-4o / gpt-4o-mini TPM in runbook §1. Tier 1 caps the verdict leg at about 4.4 to 5.2 compares per minute, so raise the tier if the launch needs more. (2) Add prepaid credit. Either turn auto-recharge on, or set a usage alert well above the expected daily spend, because an exhausted balance is exactly how this outage happened. (3) Create a NEW project key (see BP-02) and set OPENAI_API_KEY on Railway web. (4) Canary: run docs/investigations/2026-09-29-session-69-state/verify_after_credits.py and one app-shaped SSE compare (product_a/product_b). Expect HTTP 200 with success:true and a non-empty recommendation, and no 429 in the Railway log. (5) Then canary the camera path with one photo.
findings.effort: 30 min dashboard work plus a 10 min canary

votes.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. App Review Guideline 2.1(a), from the fetched copy in scratchpad/guidelines.html, says: "include demo account info (and turn on your back-end service!)". It also says: "We will reject incomplete app bundles and binaries that crash or exhibit obvious technical problems." Comparing products is the app's only core feature. A reviewer who runs a compare, whether by text pair, stream or camera, gets an error every time. That is a rejection under 2.1, so blocker is the right severity.

The cited evidence checks out:
- api.ts:764-780 sends product_a/product_b to /api/v1/text/compare/stream.
- image_routes.py:289-296 catches any Exception from identify_products and raises HTTP 500 "Image analysis failed. Please try again."
- backend_prod_measurements.txt and pair_stream.txt contain the measured INSUFFICIENT_DATA after 31.2 s and STREAM_TIMEOUT after 33.17 s.

The owner, ahmed, is also right. Topping up credits, setting a new key and changing the Railway env all need money, a dashboard or a credential. On the user's Anthropic question: the backend has no Anthropic path. A grep for anthropic in app/services/llm_provider.py, model_config.py and the app/ tree found nothing, so Anthropic credits alone would not fix this without a code change.

Two caveats on how the finding attributes cause:
1. The OpenAI 429 on the pair and stream paths is inferred, not measured. The stream log shows api_calls:0, and progress stopped at 20 ("Fetching specs and prices"). The same measurement file records a 24,042 ms event-loop stall on /health at 21:55:38Z, inside the stream's timeout window. Credits are needed, but they may not be enough to make the stream path finish in time.
2. The claim that the URL-compare path returns LLM_UNAVAILABLE has no measurement cited in the finding.

So the canary in fix step 4 is required, not optional, before the submission is treated as unblocked.
votes.corrected_claim:
This is a blocker under Guideline 2.1(a), and the owner is ahmed. OpenAI is the only LLM provider the backend calls, and it returns 429 insufficient_quota. The q= compare path was measured failing (HTTP 400), and the camera path turns any vision exception into HTTP 500 (image_routes.py:289-296). The app's own explicit-pair GET and SSE stream paths were measured failing too, with INSUFFICIENT_DATA after 31.2 s and STREAM_TIMEOUT after 33.2 s with api_calls:0. Tying those two failures to the 429 is inferred, not proven. A 24 s event-loop stall was also recorded in the same window.

Adding OpenAI credits is required. Anthropic credits would not help without code changes, because the backend has no Anthropic provider. After the new key is set, run a canary with an app-shaped SSE pair compare (success:true in under ~30 s) and one camera compare. Without that canary, the reviewer's path is not known to work.

votes.reasoning:
The facts in the finding are mostly correct, but it is not a submission problem, and "high" overstates the risk.

What I confirmed:
- I re-measured the chain on 2026-09-29 with openssl s_client -showcerts, then SPKI to SHA-256 to base64. The chain is leaf *.up.railway.app (issuer YE2), then YE2 (s/tdAOmUzd8syaTuqfgGvFcn6DzA5Cmb+Vby1ST+U3Y=), then Root YE cross-signed by X2 (sCkq5UWXjg+7mKu9lMhhYF5bGLsy7VI/UNW3tccdR7w=), then ISRG Root X2 cross-signed by X1 (diGVwiVYbubAI3RW4hB9xU8e/CH2GnkuvVFZE8zmgzI=).
- certificatePinning.ts:27-44,53-62 on main eed4ee10 pins X2, X1, YE1, E7, E8 and E5. Only X2 appears in the served chain.
- No expirationDate is set.
- There is no addSslPinningErrorListener. The only Sentry call is for init failure (certificatePinning.ts:78-82).
- On iOS the library uses TrustKit (node_modules/react-native-ssl-public-key-pinning/ios/SslPublicKeyPinning.mm:3,61). TrustKit matches pins against the chain that SecTrust validated. So if a later iOS release trusts Root YE directly, the path can stop at Root YE, no pin matches, and every backend call fails. The failure mechanism is real.

Why it does not block submission:
- The App Store binary works today. The reviewer's network flow will pass pin validation through X2. Nothing in the App Review Guidelines or ASC rejects an app for its pin set.
- The trigger is far off. letsencrypt.org/certificates says of the Gen-Y roots: "These roots are not yet included in Root Program Trust Stores, but will be submitted for inclusion soon". They have not even been submitted yet. Apple then has to review them and ship them in an iOS trust-store update. For comparison, ISRG Root X2 took about two years to reach iOS.
- The RSA side is also covered. Let's Encrypt lists YR1 and YR2 as active intermediates, and "Root YR ... Cross-signed by ISRG Root X1". X1 is pinned, so a switch to RSA issuance is covered the same way X2 covers ECDSA.
- It can be fixed without a new binary. Pins are set from JavaScript (api.ts:23), and TrustKit only enforces the pinned domain web-production-58776.up.railway.app. expo-updates fetches from u.expo.dev, which is not pinned, so a production-channel OTA can ship a corrected pin set even to a bricked install.

Corrections to the claim:
- YE1 is not "no longer served" in general. Let's Encrypt says "The four intermediates currently in active rotation are: YE1, YE2, YR1, and YR2". This leaf just happens to be issued by YE2, and a future renewal could use YE1 again. The file comment calling YE1 "Primary" is still stale.

The owner is right: this is a small JS and test change Claude can make. It is worth doing before the production build as cheap hardening, especially the Sentry pin-failure listener and the YE2 and Root YE pins. It should be medium, not high.
votes.corrected_claim:
The live chain for web-production-58776.up.railway.app, measured 2026-09-29, is leaf (issuer YE2), then YE2, then Root YE (cross-signed by X2), then ISRG Root X2 (cross-signed by X1). Of the six pins in certificatePinning.ts:53-62, only ISRG_ROOT_X2 appears in that chain. For today's App Store binary and the reviewer's flow, that one pin is enough. It also covers every active ECDSA intermediate (YE1, YE2), and the X1 pin covers the RSA ones (YR1, YR2 via Root YR cross-signed by X1).

The latent risk is that a future iOS trust-store update trusts ISRG Root YE or Root YR directly. Let's Encrypt has not yet submitted those roots to any root program. iOS path building could then end at Root YE, no pin would match, and every backend call would fail.

The pins never expire, and no addSslPinningErrorListener reports a mismatch to Sentry. Pins are set from JavaScript and expo-updates' host is not pinned, so an OTA on the production channel can fix a broken pin set without resubmission.

Hardening before the production build (owner claude, effort S):
- Pin YE2 and Root YE, plus YE1, YE3, YR1-3 and Root YR from the Let's Encrypt PEMs.
- Fix the stale "YE1 = primary" comment.
- Send pin failures to Sentry.
- Extend the jest pin test.

This is not an App Store rejection risk, and it is not a near-term outage.

votes.reasoning:
All the evidence checks out, but calling it "high" overstates how close the risk is.

Checked against main eed4ee10:
- The pin list quote at SmartCompareApp/src/services/certificatePinning.ts:53-62 is exact. So is the constant at :31 (LE_YE1_INTERMEDIATE = 'brzvtCELCIZUo4sD/…'). The comment at :58 reads "Primary: Let's Encrypt YE1 (current active issuer, issued by ISRG Root YE)".
- I re-ran openssl s_client -showcerts against web-production-58776.up.railway.app:443 on 2026-09-29. The server sends four certificates:
  - leaf *.up.railway.app, issued by YE2
  - YE2, SPKI s/tdAOmUzd8syaTuqfgGvFcn6DzA5Cmb+Vby1ST+U3Y=
  - Root YE, issued by ISRG Root X2, SPKI sCkq5UWXjg+7mKu9lMhhYF5bGLsy7VI/UNW3tccdR7w=
  - ISRG Root X2, issued by X1, SPKI diGVwiVYbubAI3RW4hB9xU8e/CH2GnkuvVFZE8zmgzI=
- Only ISRG_ROOT_X2 matches a certificate in that chain. YE1 is not served, so the "current active issuer" comment is stale.
- The letsencrypt.org/certificates page does contain "These roots are not yet included in Root Program Trust Stores, but will be submitted for inclusion soon". It also lists the chains EE←YE2←Root YE←ISRG Root X2, and EE←YE2←Root YE on its own.
- README.md:127 in react-native-ssl-public-key-pinning says "If this is not set, then the pins do not expire."
- A grep for addSslPinningErrorListener in src and App.tsx returns zero hits.
- api.ts calls setupCertificatePinning() at module load without await.
- On iOS the library depends on TrustKit (per its podspec). TrustKit checks pins against the chain that iOS verified. Once Root YE is a trusted anchor, that chain can end at Root YE and leave X2 out, so the mechanism the finding describes is plausible.

Why "high" is too strong:
- Nothing fails today. X2 is in the served chain, iOS trusts it, and the pin matches.
- The failure needs Apple to add Root YE to the iOS trust store and ship that in an iOS update. Let's Encrypt has not even submitted the root yet, and root-program inclusion usually takes many months to years.
- It is not an App Review rejection and not a launch-day outage.
- The pins are set from JavaScript, and the OTA host u.expo.dev is not pinned, so an OTA on the production channel can fix it without a new binary.

Given the S effort and the potential for a full outage, it is a worthwhile hardening task to do before the production build, but medium, not high. One part of the claim is inference, not measurement: that iOS path building would stop at Root YE and drop X2.

The live issuer YE2 (s/tdAOmUzd8syaTuqfgGvFcn6DzA5Cmb+Vby1ST+U3Y=) and ISRG Root YE (sCkq5UWXjg+7mKu9lMhhYF5bGLsy7VI/UNW3tccdR7w=) are not pinned. The comment at :58 calling YE1 the "current active issuer" is stale. The app works today because X2 is in the chain that iOS verifies. This becomes a total-outage risk later: Let's Encrypt says Root YE "will be submitted" to root programs, and if an iOS release trusts it directly, the verified chain can end at Root YE without X2. No pin would match and every backend call would fail. The pins have no expirationDate and no addSslPinningErrorListener is wired, so the failure would be silent. Because the pins are set from JavaScript and u.expo.dev is not pinned, an OTA could fix it. That makes this a medium-severity hardening item, not an imminent launch blocker. Fix: pin YE2 and Root YE (and ideally YE1/YE3/YR* and Root YR), update the comment, and send pin errors to Sentry.

votes.reasoning: Most of the evidence holds, but two parts of the claim go further than the evidence. What checks out: (1) scratchpad/backend_prod_measurements.txt lines 1-4 record the pair GET returning HTTP 400 INSUFFICIENT_DATA in 31.2 s, and the SSE stream timing out at 33.9 s. pair_stream.txt carries the quoted STREAM_TIMEOUT events word for word, with "api_calls": 0. (2) SmartCompareApp/src/services/api.ts:760-781 sets product_a/product_b and calls /api/v1/text/compare/stream, as quoted. (3) app/api/image_routes.py:288-296 wraps identify_products in `except Exception` and raises a 500 "Image analysis failed. Please try again." In app/services/openai_service.py:215-240, identify_products calls guarded_llm_create outside any try; its only try/except catches JSONDecodeError on the parse. So a 429 does surface as a 500. (4) url_extraction_service.py:658-665 returns LLM_UNAVAILABLE when generate_comparison errors. (5) docs/investigations/2026-09-29-session-69-state.md line 13 quotes the 429 insufficient_quota/credit_balance_exhausted log, three attempts per call. The core point stands: OpenAI is exhausted, the q= path fails with a logged 429, and the camera and URL paths depend on the LLM by code. That makes the reviewer-facing compare broken, so blocker is the right severity. What goes too far: (a) nothing ties the two measured app-shaped paths to OpenAI. The finding cites no Railway log line for them. INSUFFICIENT_DATA (structured_comparison_service.py:3935-3947) fires only when both products' Phase 1 fetches return None for specs AND price. The price leg is mostly scraping (Serper/Scrape.do/Bright Data), so its failure is not shown to come from the LLM. The same measurement file also records /health loop_lag_max_ms 24042 during these calls, a 24 s event-loop stall, which could explain the SSE STREAM_TIMEOUT on its own ("api_calls": 0, stopped at "Fetching specs and prices"). So "retrying cannot help" and the idea that credits alone will fix these paths are inference. (b) The camera and URL outcomes come from reading the code, not from measurement. The fix is still right because its step-4 canary covers the pair SSE, but the claim should not promise that credits restore the pair paths.
votes.corrected_claim: OpenAI returns 429 insufficient_quota (logged at extraction_service.parse_product_query), so the q= compare path fails with HTTP 400 BAD_REQUEST. By code, the camera path fails too: identify_products has no guard around the LLM call, so image_routes.py:288-296 returns a 500 "Image analysis failed". The URL compare fails as well, returning LLM_UNAVAILABLE. The app's own explicit-pair paths also fail in prod: the GET returned HTTP 400 INSUFFICIENT_DATA in 31.2 s, and the SSE returned STREAM_TIMEOUT in 33.9 s with api_calls 0. For these two paths, OpenAI is not yet proven as the sole cause. INSUFFICIENT_DATA needs specs AND prices to be None for both products, and the price leg is mostly scrape-based. A 24 s event-loop stall (loop_lag_max_ms 24042) was recorded during the same window. A reviewer running the core feature sees it fail (Guideline 2.1). Blocker. After adding credits and rotating the key, the canary must re-run the product_a/product_b GET and SSE and confirm success:true. If they still fail, investigate the price leg and the loop stall separately.

findings.title: The certificate pins do not include the intermediate or root that the backend serves today. One pin, ISRG Root X2, is what keeps the app working, and that coverage can disappear when Apple adds ISRG Root YE to its trust store.
findings.claim: I measured the live chain for web-production-58776.up.railway.app on 2026-09-29. It runs leaf (*.up.railway.app, issuer YE2), then Let's Encrypt YE2, then ISRG Root YE (cross-signed by X2), then ISRG Root X2 (cross-signed by X1). Of the six pins in certificatePinning.ts, only ISRG_ROOT_X2 matches a certificate in that chain. YE1, which the file calls the 'current active issuer', is no longer served. YE2 and Root YE are not pinned. Let's Encrypt says the Gen-Y roots 'will be submitted for inclusion soon' in root stores. Once iOS trusts Root YE directly, its path building can stop at Root YE and leave X2 out. Then no pin matches, and every backend call fails with a network error. That is the same failure as the documented 2026-07-06 outage, this time on the App Store binary. The pins have no expirationDate, so they never lapse, and nothing listens for pin errors, so a mismatch would not show up in Sentry. Pins are set from JavaScript (api.ts:23, not awaited), so an OTA on the production channel is how a broken pin set would be fixed. See BP-05.

LE_YE1_INTERMEDIATE = 'brzvtCELCIZUo4sD/qPX0ccRtPsd3DY6RfmxpOU9oB4=' ... // Primary: Let's Encrypt YE1 (current active issuer

These roots are not yet included in Root Program Trust Stores, but will be submitted for inclusion soon

findings.fix: Do this before the production build. Add pins for LE YE2 (s/tdAOmUzd8syaTuqfgGvFcn6DzA5Cmb+Vby1ST+U3Y=) and ISRG Root YE (sCkq5UWXjg+7mKu9lMhhYF5bGLsy7VI/UNW3tccdR7w=). Also add YE1, YE3, YR1, YR2, YR3 and ISRG Root YR, deriving those hashes from the PEMs on letsencrypt.org with the openssl runbook in the file header. Fix the stale 'YE1 = primary' comment. Wire addSslPinningErrorListener to Sentry.captureMessage so a mismatch is visible. Extend the jest pin test to assert that the live-chain hashes are present.

findings.title: supportsTablet=true makes it a native iPad app: 13-inch iPad screenshots required, iPad review, and landscape/multitasking with no iPad layout work
findings.claim: With supportsTablet true, the generated Info.plist allows all four iPad orientations and UIRequiresFullScreen=false, so the app must work in landscape and Split View on iPad. Apple then requires 13-inch iPad screenshots, and the reviewer may test on an iPad. The code has no iPad handling: zero isPad hits, and ScannerReticle captures the window width once at module load, so it goes stale on rotation or split. For v1, supportsTablet=false keeps the app on iPad in iPhone-compatibility mode: no iPad screenshots, and nothing in the iPad layout to review. Note that app.json 'orientation: portrait' constrains the iPhone only.

const VIEWPORT_WIDTH = Dimensions.get('window').width;
Required if app runs on iPad ... 2064 x 2752 pixels (portrait)

findings.fix: Recommend setting ios.supportsTablet to false in app.json before the first production build. It is a one-line change Claude can make, but the product call is Ahmed's. If iPad stays, budget for iPad QA in landscape and Split View plus 13-inch screenshots. The change is native and needs the build.

votes.reasoning:
I checked the claim against Apple's primary sources and it holds.

1. **The config is as stated.** SmartCompareApp/app.json:18 has `"supportsTablet": true`, and app.json:6 has `"orientation": "portrait"`. With supportsTablet true, Expo lists iPad (device family 2) as a supported device. The orchestrator's introspect evidence shows all four iPad orientations and UIRequiresFullScreen=false. That matches Apple's multitasking rule: an iPad app that supports multitasking must declare all four orientations or upload validation fails with ITMS-90474.

2. **iPad screenshots are required.** Apple's screenshot specifications page (https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/reference/screenshot-specifications/) lists the 13-inch iPad size (2064 x 2752 or 2048 x 2732 portrait) as "Required if app runs on iPad". App Store Connect applies this to binaries that declare iPad support. An iPhone-only binary running on iPad in compatibility mode does not need iPad screenshots. So with the current config, the version cannot be submitted until 13-inch iPad screenshots are uploaded. They would also have to show the app in use (Guideline 2.3.3).

3. **Layout risk is real.** Reviewers test a universal app on iPad. The code has no iPad handling. A grep of src/ finds only `Dimensions.get('window').width` at ScannerReticle.tsx:15 (module-level const, captured once) and SlideTransition.tsx:50, and there are no isPad or useWindowDimensions hits. Portrait-only layouts forced into landscape or Split View are a common source of Guideline 2.1 and 4.0 rejections.

4. **The mitigation is right.** Guideline 2.4.1 says "iPhone apps should run on iPad whenever possible". With supportsTablet=false the app still runs on iPad in compatibility mode, so 2.4.1 is satisfied and neither iPad screenshots nor the iPad layout come into play. The reviewer may still open it on an iPad, but only in the iPhone-sized window.

5. **One point missing from the finding.** Choosing iPad support on the first submitted build is effectively one-way. Once a version with iPad support is released, App Store Connect rejects later builds that drop a device family the previous version supported. So this has to be decided before the first production build.

**Severity: high is correct, not blocker.** Missing iPad screenshots stop the submission from being sent, but that is a prep item rather than an Apple rejection, and the iPad layout problem is a likely rejection, not a certain one.

**Owner: "either" is correct.** The one-line edit is Claude's to make; the product call is Ahmed's. It needs a native build, not an OTA update.

Nothing in the code handles iPad: there are no isPad or useWindowDimensions hits, and ScannerReticle.tsx:15 captures the window width once at module load. findings.title: OpenAI retry knobs are unset: 3 attempts per call, 6 per verdict chain, and the SSE verdict tail is unbounded
findings.claim: Neither OPENAI_MAX_RETRIES nor OPENAI_FALLBACK_MAX_RETRIES is in the Railway web variable names, so the SDK default of 2 retries applies. The runbook's launch setting of 1/0 gives 3. ENABLE_FULL_STREAM_DEADLINE is also unset, so the streaming verdict, critique and moderation tail runs outside STREAM_HARD_CAP_SECONDS. The runbook models a single SSE connection being held for about 6.5 minutes under degradation, or about 13 minutes for the worst chain. ENABLE_PREVERDICT_DISCONNECT_ABORT is also unset, so the tail is paid for even after the client has left. The runbook calls ENABLE_FULL_STREAM_DEADLINE 'a hard pairing with OpenAI re-funding'. On the local SDK source (2.21.0; the pinned version is 3.3.1, not measured), _should_retry retries every 429 unless the server sends x-should-retry:false.

findings.title: Push notifications need an APNs key on EAS credentials; the build step can skip it silently
findings.claim: The client registers Expo push tokens, and the backend has re-engagement pushes (ENABLE_REENGAGEMENT_PUSHES is set on Railway). For the Expo push service to deliver to a store build, an APNs key must be attached to the project's iOS credentials. If 'set up Push Notifications' is declined at the production build, or was never done for the preview builds, getExpoPushTokenAsync still succeeds but every send fails. Whether a push key exists could not be measured, because eas credentials is interactive. The entitlement shows aps-environment=development from the expo-notifications plugin default. That is normal for managed builds: App Store export signing uses the distribution profile, so this is not a finding by itself.

"expo-notifications", { "color": "#10B981" }
"aps-environment": "development"

findings.fix: During the EXPO-02 credential session, run `eas credentials -p ios` and confirm or create a Push Notifications key. Then send one test push through the Expo push tool to a TestFlight install before submitting.
findings.effort: 10 min in the same Hussain session

votes.reasoning:
The technical claim holds, but it is not a submission problem.

1. Delivery needs an APNs key. Expo's push-notifications-setup doc (https://docs.expo.dev/push-notifications/push-notifications-setup/) says the first EAS build asks to "Setup Push Notifications for your project" and to generate "a new Apple Push Notifications service key". If you run `eas credentials` without EAS Build, you do it by hand. So if that prompt was declined, or a non-interactive run skipped it, the app still gets a token but sends to it fail. That matches the finding.

2. The client handles a failure without breaking the app. In SmartCompareApp/src/services/pushTokenService.ts:61-95, each step returns {registered:false, reason} instead of throwing: the permission check, `getExpoPushTokenAsync` at line 77, and the backend PUT. The backend sends through Expo at app/services/push_service.py:22 (`_EXPO_PUSH_URL = "https://exp.host/--/api/v2/push/send"`). A missing APNs key therefore causes failures on the server side, which a reviewer never sees.

3. Apple policy. App Review Guideline 4.5.4 (https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/) says "Push Notifications must not be required for the app to function". A compliant app has to work fully with no push delivery at all. Pushes that never arrive cannot trigger a rejection, and the reviewer does not exercise push delivery. The `aps-environment=development` entitlement also does not count against it, as the finding itself says.

4. Other points. The value of ENABLE_REENGAGEMENT_PUSHES on Railway is unknown: the variable is set, but no value was measured. So the claim that re-engagement pushes are live in prod is not established. Whether an APNs key already exists is also unmeasured; one may have been created when the preview builds were set up.

5. Owner. `ahmed` is correct. Creating or confirming the key needs the Apple team credentials (Hussain Aseeri, individual team 8K562M549D) through an interactive `eas credentials` or `eas build` session.

Conclusion: the finding is a valid pre-launch check, but it causes no rejection and no failure in the review flow. It is a silent loss of a secondary engagement feature, so severity drops from medium to low.

A related Apple point this finding does not raise: 4.5.4 also requires explicit in-app opt-in and an opt-out for promotional pushes. If the "re-engagement" pushes are marketing, that is the real policy exposure, and it belongs in its own finding.

findings.title: Arabic not declared as a bundle localization (CFBundleLocalizations absent), and purpose strings are English-only
findings.claim: The app ships Arabic UI and runtime forceRTL, but the Info.plist declares no supported localizations and there is no `locales` block. As a result, the App Store 'Languages' row will list English only, and iOS system text (permission alerts, the native Apple sign-in sheet chrome) stays English for Arabic users. RTL itself works through the runtime I18nManager.forceRTL, so this is metadata and polish, not a crash.

if (mergedConfig?.supportsRTL == null && mergedConfig?.forcesRTL == null && supportedLocales == null) return config;
I18nManager.allowRTL(true); I18nManager.forceRTL(shouldBeRTL);

findings.fix: Set ["expo-localization", {"supportedLocales": ["en","ar"]}] (writes CFBundleLocalizations). Optionally add expo.locales with an ar.json holding the Arabic camera and photo purpose strings, reviewed by the same native Arabic reviewer as the 51 labels. This is native and must go in before the build.

votes.reasoning:
I checked the evidence and it holds. SmartCompareApp/app.json:179 adds "expo-localization" as a bare string with no options. The plugin's early return in node_modules/expo-localization/plugin/build/withExpoLocalization.js:14-17 therefore fires, so CFBundleLocalizations is never written. ios.infoPlist at app.json:128-130 contains only ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption, and app.json has no `locales` key. The only purpose strings are the English literals at app.json:183 (cameraPermission) and :191 (photosPermission). App.tsx:196-198 flips RTL at runtime when the saved language is 'ar'. The same gap was raised earlier in docs/investigations/2026-09-06-full-review-state/critic-m22-mobile.md:9 and was never fixed.

Nothing in the App Review Guidelines requires an app's binary to be localized into the languages of its UI or its storefront. Expo's localization guide (docs.expo.dev/guides/localization) describes both mechanisms as optional polish. `supportedLocales` lets users pick the app's language per app in system settings, and `locales` with CFBundleAllowMixedLocalizations lets you "provide localized strings for things like the display name and system dialogs". To translate permission messages, "add the matching usage-description key to the `ios` object in each locale file". The App Store Connect localization page covers only metadata localization and does not tie the product-page languages to Info.plist. 1. The claim that CFBundleLocalizations alone makes the App Store "Languages" row show Arabic is not proven. I could not find Apple primary-source text on how the row is derived. The finding is right that this is native config and has to land before the one production eas build, or a second build will be needed.

findings.title: The Sentry source-map phase fails the whole iOS build if SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN is invalid
findings.claim: SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN exists by name in the EAS production environment (measured), so the build is configured. But sentry-xcode.sh exits 1 on any sentry-cli failure (a revoked or expired token, or a de.sentry.io outage) unless SENTRY_ALLOW_FAILURE is set. That makes the store build hostage to Sentry. The last successful iOS build was 2026-07-04, so the token has not been exercised in almost three months.

evidence.quote: Environment: production / SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN=<redacted>
echo "error: sentry-cli - To disable source maps auto upload, set SENTRY_DISABLE_AUTO_UPLOAD=true ... Or to allow failing upload, set SENTRY_ALLOW_FAILURE=true" ... exitCode=1

findings.fix: Optionally add SENTRY_ALLOW_FAILURE=true as a plain EAS env var in production so an upload failure warns instead of failing the build. If the first production build fails in the bundle phase, check the Sentry token first.

votes.reasoning:
The mechanism holds. Seen from Apple's side, though, this is not a submission or review problem. Nothing in the App Review Guidelines or App Store Connect looks at Sentry: this can only fail the EAS build before anything reaches ASC. So "low" is the right severity.

Evidence:
- The Sentry build script is wired in. SmartCompareApp/app.json:221-226 declares the @sentry/react-native plugin (url https://de.sentry.io/, organization qaren-rr, project react-native). node_modules/@sentry/react-native/plugin/build/withSentryIOS.js:30 and :61 inject sentry-xcode.sh into the "Bundle React Native code and images" build phase at prebuild. The installed version is 7.2.0, and package.json:22 pins ~7.2.0.
- The script fails the build on an upload error. sentry-xcode.sh:51-61 runs `sentry-cli react-native xcode` unless SENTRY_DISABLE_AUTO_UPLOAD=true. On a non-zero exit it prints "error: sentry-cli - ... Or to allow failing upload, set SENTRY_ALLOW_FAILURE=true" and sets exitCode=1. Line 75 then runs `exit $exitCode`, so the bundle phase fails and the whole iOS build fails with it.
- The proposed fix works. SENTRY_ALLOW_FAILURE is read by sentry-cli itself, so setting it makes the upload failure non-fatal. SENTRY_DISABLE_AUTO_UPLOAD=true is the harder switch that skips the upload entirely.
- eas.json sets no SENTRY_* variable in any profile (grep returns nothing). The build therefore depends on the EAS production environment variable the finding measured.

Where the claim overreaches:
- "Not exercised in almost three months" is speculative. Sentry organization auth tokens do not expire by default. The real risks are a revoked or wrong-scope token, or a de.sentry.io outage.
- We don't know that the 2026-07-04 preview build used this production-environment token at all.

It can never cause an Apple rejection or break a reviewer's flow. At worst it costs one failed build and a rerun (about 30 minutes of EAS build time) before a first production build that has never happened, so it is a launch-day nuisance rather than an outage.

On owner: "either" is right. Ahmed can add the variable in the EAS dashboard. Claude could run `eas env:create`, but that changes project configuration, so it needs Ahmed's approval.

That script exits 1 if sentry-cli fails to upload source maps (sentry-xcode.sh:51-61, 75) unless SENTRY_ALLOW_FAILURE=true or SENTRY_DISABLE_AUTO_UPLOAD=true is set. A revoked or wrong-scope SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN, or a de.sentry.io outage, would therefore fail the EAS production build. This is not an App Review or App Store Connect issue: it costs a rebuild, not a rejection. The token's age alone is not evidence of failure, because Sentry org tokens do not expire by default. Optional mitigation: set SENTRY_ALLOW_FAILURE=true in the EAS production environment. If the first build fails in "Bundle React Native code and images", check the Sentry token first.

findings.title: Outage failures are mislabelled as the user's fault; ENABLE_LLM_PREFLIGHT_BREAKER would give a clean 503 LLM_UNAVAILABLE and stop the Bright Data spend, but has a trip-on-TPM trade-off

findings.title: Supabase free-plan pause risk: the project was paused once, and /health (the Railway healthcheck) never touches Supabase

findings.title: The notification permission prompt fires right at first login with no explanation, and re-engagement (marketing) pushes are enabled
findings.claim: tryRegisterPushToken runs on every authenticated launch and at login. It calls requestPermissionsAsync directly, so the reviewer gets the iOS prompt with no context. ENABLE_REENGAGEMENT_PUSHES is set on Railway. Guideline 4.5.4 requires explicit in-app opt-in consent wording for promotional pushes.

evidence.quote: const existing = await Notifications.getPermissionsAsync(); ... const requested = await Notifications.requestPermissionsAsync();
tryRegisterPushToken().catch(() => { /* never blocks app boot */ });
should not be used for promotions or direct marketing purposes unless customers have explicitly opted in

findings.fix: Claude: delay the permission request until after the first successful compare, behind a short pre-prompt that explains what the notifications are for. Confirm the Profile re-engagement toggle has opt-in wording and a working opt-out.

votes.reasoning:
This is not a submission problem, but the sequencing bug inside it is real.

1) What the guideline says. Guideline 4.5.4 (fetched from developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/) reads: "Push Notifications should not be used for promotions or direct marketing purposes unless customers have explicitly opted in to receive them via consent language displayed in your app's UI, and you provide a method in your app for a user to opt out". It says nothing about when the iOS permission prompt may appear. Asking at launch or login is common, and the guidelines do not forbid it. Apple's Requesting Permission page is advice, not a rule reviewers enforce.

2) The app already meets 4.5.4.
- **Consent language exists.** Onboarding step 17 is an in-app consent screen. SmartCompareApp/src/screens/onboarding/Step17Notifications.tsx:52 calls requestPermissionsAsync only after the user taps "Allow notifications". Its copy (en.json:686-697) explains what the notifications are: "at most one helpful nudge per week", decision insights, cohort echoes and price-drop shortcuts.
- **Opt-out exists.** ProfileScreen.tsx has a notifications master toggle (handleNotificationsToggle, PUT /preference-toggles) and three per-category toggles (handleSubToggle, PUT /reengagement-subs).
- **The pushes are not really marketing.** The payloads in app/services/reengagement_service.py (about lines 305-375) cover the user's own saved comparison ("new reviews shifted the picture"), a cohort nudge, and a 14-day look back at the user's own decision. None of them promotes a third-party offer.

3) The finding overstates two things.
- ENABLE_REENGAGEMENT_PUSHES is only known to be set as a variable name on Railway. Its value is unknown, and the gate at reengagement_service.py:33-39 needs a truthy string, so "enabled" is not proven.
- "No explanation" ignores step 17.

4) What is true. App.tsx:313 (onLoginSuccess) and App.tsx:238 (every authenticated launch) both call tryRegisterPushToken. At pushTokenService.ts:62-64 that function calls requestPermissionsAsync whenever the status is not 'granted'. Onboarding only renders after sign-in (App.tsx:364-370: `!isAuthenticated ? … : needsPreferences ? …`). So on a fresh install the iOS system prompt appears right at signup/login, before the step 17 screen. That makes step 17 mostly pointless and costs opt-in rate. The code comment claims the function only asks when the status is undetermined, but the code does not check for that.

That is a UX and conversion bug, not something Apple would reject. The owner "either" is right; this is a small code change Claude can make.
votes.corrected_claim:
This will not cause an App Store rejection; it is a low-severity UX bug. tryRegisterPushToken (SmartCompareApp/src/services/pushTokenService.ts:62-64) calls Notifications.requestPermissionsAsync whenever the status is not 'granted', and it runs at login (App.tsx:313) and on every authenticated launch (App.tsx:238). Onboarding only renders after sign-in (App.tsx:364-370), so the iOS system prompt fires before the step 17 consent screen (Step17Notifications.tsx:52, copy at en.json:686-697) is ever shown. That makes step 17 mostly pointless and lowers opt-in.

Guideline 4.5.4 is already met: step 17 shows consent language, ProfileScreen has a master opt-out plus three per-category toggles, and the re-engagement payloads (reengagement_service.py ~305-375) are about the user's own comparisons, not promotions. Whether ENABLE_REENGAGEMENT_PUSHES is actually on is unknown; only the variable name is known to be set.

Fix (Claude, about 30-60 min): in tryRegisterPushToken, register the token only if the permission is already granted. Leave the request to the step 17 "Allow" path, then register the token right after a grant. Update the stale comment and the jest pins that go with it.

votes.reasoning:
I checked the evidence against main (now 89f2dc6a). The quotes are real and in the places cited.
- SmartCompareApp/src/services/pushTokenService.ts:62-64 calls getPermissionsAsync, and if the status is not 'granted' it calls requestPermissionsAsync directly, with nothing shown first.
- SmartCompareApp/App.tsx:238 calls it on every authenticated launch and App.tsx:313 in handleLoginSuccess, right after setIsAuthenticated(true).

On a fresh install the permission status is undetermined, so the bare iOS prompt appears at first login. That is before the user reaches onboarding, since needsPreferences sends a new user there.

The finding leaves out mitigating context that weakens the 4.5.4 "marketing" part:
1. An explained pre-prompt already exists. SmartCompareApp/src/screens/onboarding/Step17Notifications.tsx:47-53 shows onboarding.s17.title/subtitle with Allow / Not now buttons ("Asked AFTER value built, not at launch", lines 4-5). The login-time call in App.tsx:313 uses up the single iOS prompt before step 17 is reached, so the real defect is that App.tsx pre-empts step 17. Nothing is missing that needs to be built.
2. An opt-out exists. ProfileScreen.tsx:207-209 has the re-engagement sub-toggles, PUT to /reengagement-subs, with the comment "Opt-OUT default by design (re-engagement chosen at onboarding step 17)".
3. The re-engagement content is not promotional as written. app/legal/terms_of_service.md:91 says "We never send price-drop spam, advertising, or promotional content". The three types are decision-insight, cohort and retrospective, with at most one per week (reengagement_service.py detectors). Calling these "marketing pushes" is an overstatement.
4. The orchestrator facts only show that ENABLE_REENGAGEMENT_PUSHES is set on Railway. Its value is unknown, and reengagement_service.py:39 enables it only for a truthy string. "Enabled" is not established.

Apple does not require a pre-prompt for the permission request, and 4.5.4 is at most arguable because an opt-in screen and an opt-out already exist. Rejection is unlikely, and low severity is right. The quote from Guideline 4.5.4 is a faithful paraphrase of the real guideline text.
votes.corrected_claim:
App.tsx:238 (every authenticated launch) and App.tsx:313 (handleLoginSuccess) call tryRegisterPushToken. That calls Notifications.requestPermissionsAsync directly (pushTokenService.ts:62-64) whenever permission is not granted. So on a fresh install the bare iOS notification prompt fires at first login, before the user reaches onboarding step 17 (Step17Notifications.tsx). That step already has an explained Allow / Not now pre-prompt, which is left useless because the one-time system prompt has already been shown.

Re-engagement pushes are gated by ENABLE_REENGAGEMENT_PUSHES. The variable name is set on Railway, but its value is unverified. The ToS describes the pushes as non-promotional (terms_of_service.md:91), and they can be switched off per type in Profile (ProfileScreen.tsx:207-209). Under 4.5.4 this is a minor risk, not a clear violation.

Fix: remove the permission request from the login and launch path. Only fetch or register the token when permission is already granted, and let Step 17 (plus an explained re-ask later, if wanted) be the only place that requests permission. Also make sure the Profile toggles' default matches the user's Step 17 answer.

The ISRG_ROOT_X2 pin diGVwiVYbubAI3RW4hB9xU8e/CH2GnkuvVFZE8zmgzI= matches the chain's X2 SPKI, so pinned builds connect.
